title: Infodemic and Fake News Turning Shift for Media: Distrust among University Students
screen_reason: Mixed-methods survey of 849 university students with a five-point frequency item on how often media outlets distribute fake news, reported both as a full frequency distribution with counts (Table 4) and as an author-stated share above threshold ('a concerning 50% of the sample associated fake news with media outlets in different levels'). Under the RECALL branch this qualifies as a perceived amount of misinformation in the respondent's information environment, with a 'how often' scale reduced to a share of respondents above a threshold. INCLUDED but flagged borderline: see the row's notes and missed_or_uncertain -- the item asks about media outlets AS DISTRIBUTORS of fake news, which is as much a media-distrust attribution as a personal-encounter report, and an adjudicator may reasonably rule it out of scope. Everything else in the paper (media trust levels, social network use frequencies, the affective framing of fake news as humour/entertainment/distrust/manipulation, and the qualitative phase) is ineligible.

estimates.country: Not stated in the text; author based at Universidad Antonio de Nebrija, Madrid, and the questionnaire collected 'country, autonomous community'
estimates.date: Not reported (article received 30 September 2022, published 2 November 2022)
estimates.measure_type: % of university students who say media outlets distribute fake news at least 'Sometimes' on a five-point never-to-always scale
estimates.value_raw: "a concerning 50% of the sample" = Sometimes 25.7% (n = 218) + Frequently 19% (n = 161) + Always 5.4% (n = 46) = 425 of 849
estimates.denominator: 849 university students (convenience sample from eight degree programmes across two faculties, Communication and Education; 40.2% undergraduate, 59.8% postgraduate; 66.8% female; mean age 26.8, SD 8.24, range 18-51)
estimates.definition: Respondent chose 'Sometimes', 'Frequently' or 'Always' rather than 'Never' or 'Rarely' on the item measuring perception of media outlets as distributors of fake news (five-point Likert, 1 = 'not at all or never', 5 = 'a lot or all')
estimates.misinfo_def: "Based on the perception of consuming and receiving misleading or incorrect information that is passed off as real information" (Table 1, definition of the 'Fake news reception and perception' construct); the paper separately defines disinformation as "intentional dissemination of non-rigorous information that seeks to undermine public trust, distort facts, convey a certain way of perceiving reality and exploit vulnerabilities with the aim of destabilizing"
estimates.source_quote: General data show that a concerning 50% of the sample associated fake news with media outlets in different levels (Sometimes, 25.7%; Frequently, 19%, and Always, 5.4%).
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.1.2 'Fake News Perceptions', p. 7 (Figure 4), with the frequency counts in Table 4, p. 8; restated in the Discussion, p. 11
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Pure self-report perception, no external verification of any kind. Instrument adapted from a previously used and validated questionnaire by the same author, reviewed by a panel of five experts who cut it from 95 to 89 items; Cronbach's alpha 0.86 for the 21-item 'Fake news reception and perception' construct (0.78 for social media consumption, 0.71 for trust). Five-point ordinal Likert response format.
estimates.moderator_quote: As for the sample under study, the chosen sampling technique was non-probabilistic and included convenience sampling, in which the sample is available at the time and during the period of the research, as Vilches [33] pointed out. A total of 849 subjects (M = 26.8; SD = 8.24; Min. = 18; Max. = 51) from eight different degrees...
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE, FLAGGED FOR ADJUDICATION. The item measures how often the respondent thinks MEDIA OUTLETS distribute fake news. Read one way that is a perceived amount of misinformation in one's information environment, which the RECALL rule explicitly admits, and the paper's own construct definition is framed as 'the perception of consuming and receiving misleading or incorrect information'. Read the other way it is a media-distrust attribution -- an opinion about who is to blame rather than a report of personal encounter -- in which case the paper yields no eligible estimate. I included it because the construct definition is about reception and because the threshold share is stated verbatim; an adjudicator may drop it. R8 is satisfied twice: the author states '50%' in the results and 'almost half' in the discussion, and the value is also an exact part/whole from the verbatim Table 4 counts (218 + 161 + 46 = 425 of 849 = 50.1%), so it is not a sum I constructed. OTHER CODING CAVEATS: the country is never stated -- Spain is inferred from the author's Madrid affiliation, the 'autonomous community' item and the Spanish-language quotations, so country_norm should be treated as an inference; no data-collection dates are given anywhere, so year is the publication year; the sample is a student convenience sample, coded general_public because students are lay respondents but explicitly NOT population-representative (the author states 'it is not representative of the population'); breadth = misleading because the construct definition's broadest term is 'misleading or incorrect'; classification_level = claim_level because the respondent is judging content, although the item's grammatical object is the outlet. Table 3's N column sums to 848, not 849.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED, ineligible. (1) The complement 'at least Rarely' (100 - 8.3 = 91.7%) is a complement I would have to compute, barred by R8, and 'Rarely' is too weak a threshold to read as a share reporting any exposure. (2) Age-slot breakdowns of the same item (Table 4 row percentages: 18-21 Sometimes 26.5 / Frequently 16.5 / Always 4.7; 22-25 26.7 / 23.9 / 6.7; 26-29 26.8 / 21.4 / 8.9; 30-35 26.6 / 26.6 / 4.7; 35-40 14.1 / 15.6 / 3.1; over 40 27.3 / 12.5 / 3.4) are demographic subgroups, not the paper's headline, so the pooled figure is kept instead. Note an unresolved internal inconsistency the adjudicator should see: the Discussion claims 'it is the youngest participants who associate this distribution the most (almost 70%)', but Table 4's own row for the 18-21 group gives 26.5 + 16.5 + 4.7 = 47.7%, and the 18-21 group is not in fact the highest on that reading -- so the narrative and the table disagree, and I trusted the table. (3) 'Fake news perceived as distrust' (undergraduates 72.7% Frequently and Always, falling to 48% among the over-40s) measures an affective/evaluative association with the concept of fake news, not exposure to it; the parallel humour, entertainment and manipulation items are reported only as non-significant p-values with no shares. (4) Media-trust distributions (Slightly: 31.8 / 37.8 / 35.7 / 29.7 / 46.9 / 42% by age slot; Very + Extremely: 21.4 / 19.5 / 16.1 / 9.4 / 17.2 / 13.6%; 'in all age slots studied, more than 40% of the sample' mistrusting; 'none of the age slots reach 5% in the category trusting extremely') are trust attitudes, not misinformation prevalence. (5) Social network use frequencies (Table 2: WhatsApp Always 56.2% and 'Frequently and Always' 81.2%, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, Twitter, YouTube) and engagement levels (Figure 2, 53.9% and 54.5% / 45.4%) are media-use measures. (6) The Spearman correlation between age and time on social networks (R = -0.516) is an association. (7) Figures 1, 2, 3 and 5 report percentages only inside images that this text extraction does not render, so any additional values they carry could not be read; the numbers quoted in the running text are all captured above. (8) The Reuters Digital News Report 2021 figures quoted in the literature review (58% concerned about what is false and real online; health-COVID-19 54%, politics 43%, celebrities 29%, climate change 20%) are cited from another publication and are barred by R8. (9) The qualitative phase (100 students, NVIVO content analysis) is qualitative-only and yields no shares.

rob.design: Cross-sectional self-administered questionnaire plus a qualitative sub-study; non-probabilistic convenience sample of 849 university students recruited from eight degree programmes in two faculties (Communication and Education) -- 341 undergraduate (40.2%), 508 postgraduate (59.8%), 66.8% female, mean age 26.8 (SD 8.24, range 18-51) -- of whom 100 took part in the semi-structured interview phase. The instrument was adapted from a previously validated questionnaire by the same author, cut from 95 to 89 items after review by five experts, organised in four blocks (sociodemographics, social media consumption, fake news perceptions, trust in social agents) with Cronbach's alpha of 0.78, 0.86 and 0.71 for the three constructs; responses are five-point ordinal Likert. Analysis in SPSS 25 (Kolmogorov-Smirnov indicated non-normality, hence Spearman correlations and chi-square) and NVIVO 10 for the qualitative data. No ethical approval was sought on the grounds that only perceptions were collected; informed consent was obtained. Substantial reporting gaps: no data-collection dates, no recruitment or response rate, no country of the sample stated, no exact question wording for the fake news items, and figures rather than tables carry several reported percentages. The author explicitly concedes the sample 'is not representative of the population'. Risk of bias is high for generalisability, and the key measure is unvalidated self-perception with a documented narrative-versus-table inconsistency in the age analysis.
